lessons.title: Articles — O, A, Os, As
lessons.explanation: Portuguese has masculine and feminine articles. Definite: o (masc. sg.), a (fem. sg.), os (masc. pl.), as (fem. pl.). Indefinite: um, uma, uns, umas.
examples: o livro (the book — masc.)
a casa (the house — fem.)
os meninos (the boys — masc. pl.)
as flores (the flowers — fem. pl.)
lessons.tip: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine; most ending in -a are feminine. Exceptions exist!

quiz.question: What is the masculine singular definite article in Portuguese?
What article goes with 'casa' (house, feminine)?

lessons.title: Ser vs. Estar
lessons.explanation: Like Spanish, Portuguese has two verbs for 'to be'. Ser: permanent characteristics, identity, origin, time, material. Estar: temporary states, location (of people/movable things), feelings.
examples: Eu sou brasileiro. (I am Brazilian.) — ser, identity
Ela está em Lisboa. (She is in Lisbon.) — estar, location
O livro é interessante. (The book is interesting.) — ser, inherent quality
Estou cansado. (I am tired.) — estar, temporary state
lessons.tip: A key difference from Spanish: 'The book is on the table' uses estar in Portuguese (Perm. location of objects often uses estar).

quiz.question: Which verb for 'I am Brazilian' (nationality)?

lessons.title: Present Tense — Regular Verbs
lessons.explanation: Portuguese verbs: -AR, -ER, -IR. -AR (falar): falo, falas, fala, falamos, falais/falam, falam. -ER (comer): como, comes, come, comemos, comeis/comem, comem. -IR (partir): parto, partes, parte, partimos, partis/partem, partem.
examples: Eu falo português. (I speak Portuguese.)
Ela come arroz. (She eats rice.)
Nós partimos amanhã. (We leave tomorrow.)
Você mora aqui? (Do you live here?)
lessons.tip: European and Brazilian Portuguese differ in second-person forms. Brazil uses você (3rd person endings) far more than tu.

quiz.question: What is the 'eu' form of 'falar'?

lessons.title: Ter — To Have
lessons.explanation: Ter (to have): tenho, tens, tem, temos, tendes/têm, têm. Used for possession and as the main auxiliary for perfect tenses in European Portuguese.
examples: Tenho dois irmãos. (I have two brothers.)
Ela tem fome. (She is hungry.) — lit. she has hunger
Tens tempo? (Do you have time?)
Temos uma reunião. (We have a meeting.)
lessons.tip: Ter is used for expressing age: Tenho quinze anos. (I am fifteen years old.)

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have' in Portuguese?

lessons.title: Preterite vs. Imperfect
lessons.explanation: Pretérito perfeito simples: completed, specific past actions. Pretérito imperfeito: habitual/ongoing past actions or background descriptions. Perfeito of falar: falei, falaste, falou, falámos, falastes, falaram.
examples: Ontem fui ao mercado. (Yesterday I went to the market.) — perfeito
Quando era criança, brincava muito. (When I was a child, I played a lot.) — imperfeito
Ela falou por uma hora. (She spoke for an hour.) — perfeito
O sol brilhava e os pássaros cantavam. (The sun was shining and birds were singing.) — imperfeito
lessons.tip: Imperfeito sets the scene; perfeito gives the events. They often appear in the same passage.

quiz.question: Which past tense describes habitual actions in the past?

lessons.title: Possessive Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Portuguese possessive adjectives (meu/minha, teu/tua, seu/sua, nosso/nossa, vosso/vossa) agree in gender and number with the noun possessed. They are often used with a definite article in European Portuguese (o meu livro), though this is optional and less common in Brazilian Portuguese.
examples: o meu livro / meu livro (my book)
a minha casa / minha casa (my house)
os teus amigos (your friends)
a nossa família (our family)
lessons.tip: 'Seu/sua' can mean his, her, its, your (formal), or their — to avoid ambiguity, speakers often use 'dele/dela' instead (o livro dele = his book).

quiz.question: Which possessive agrees with a feminine singular noun meaning 'my'?
What alternative avoids ambiguity with 'seu/sua'?

lessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
lessons.explanation: Portuguese comparatives use mais/menos...do que (more/less...than) or tão...como (as...as). Superlatives use o/a/os/as mais/menos + adjective. Irregular comparatives: bom→melhor, mau→pior, grande→maior, pequeno→menor.
examples: Ela é mais alta do que eu. (She is taller than me.)
Este livro é tão interessante como aquele. (This book is as interesting as that one.)
É o aluno mais inteligente da turma. (He is the smartest student in the class.)
Este bolo é melhor do que o outro. (This cake is better than the other.)
lessons.tip: 'Do que' (than) is used after mais/menos, even though 'que' alone is common in casual Brazilian speech.

quiz.question: How do you say 'more...than' in Portuguese?
What is the irregular comparative of 'bom'?

lessons.title: Contractions — Prepositions with Articles
lessons.explanation: Portuguese contracts common prepositions with definite and indefinite articles into single words: de+o=do, de+a=da, em+o=no, em+a=na, a+o=ao, a+a=à. These contractions are mandatory in standard Portuguese.
examples: Venho do Brasil. (I come from Brazil.) — de + o
Ela está na escola. (She is at school.) — em + a
Vou ao mercado. (I'm going to the market.) — a + o
O livro está na mesa. (The book is on the table.) — em + a
lessons.tip: These contractions are required, not optional — you cannot say 'de o Brasil'; it must be 'do Brasil.'

quiz.question: What is the contraction of 'em' + 'a'?
What is the contraction of 'de' + 'o'?

lessons.title: Personal Infinitive — A Unique Portuguese Feature
lessons.explanation: Portuguese has a personal infinitive (infinitivo pessoal) that conjugates. It adds personal endings to the infinitive: falar, falares, falar, falarmos, falardes, falarem. Used in many subordinate clause structures.
examples: É importante estudares. (It is important for you to study.)
Antes de sairmos, come. (Before we leave, eat.)
Para eles virem, precisam de vistos. (For them to come, they need visas.)
Depois de ela chegar, começamos. (After she arrives, we begin.)
lessons.tip: The personal infinitive is unique to Portuguese. It allows you to have a clear subject in an infinitive clause.

quiz.question: What is special about the Portuguese personal infinitive?
options: it is only used in Brazil

lessons.title: Reflexive Verbs
lessons.explanation: Portuguese reflexive verbs use reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nos, vos, se) that usually precede the verb in Brazilian Portuguese, but can follow with a hyphen in European Portuguese (levantar-se). Common reflexives: levantar-se, vestir-se, chamar-se.
examples: Eu me levanto às sete. (I get up at seven.) — Brazilian
Ela chama-se Ana. (Her name is Ana.) — European
Nós nos vestimos rápido. (We get dressed quickly.)
Você se lembra disso? (Do you remember that?)
lessons.tip: Brazilian Portuguese usually places the pronoun before the verb (me levanto); European Portuguese often attaches it after with a hyphen (levanto-me).

quiz.question: Which pronoun goes with 'nós' in reflexive verbs?
Where does European Portuguese often place the reflexive pronoun?
options: at the end of the sentence only

lessons.title: Futuro do Presente — Future Tense
lessons.explanation: The simple future is formed by adding endings (-ei, -ás, -á, -emos, -eis, -ão) directly to the infinitive, the same for all three verb groups. Three common verbs have irregular stems: fazer→far-, dizer→dir-, trazer→trar-.
examples: Falarei com ela amanhã. (I will speak with her tomorrow.)
Você virá à festa? (Will you come to the party?)
Teremos uma reunião. (We will have a meeting.)
Eles farão o trabalho. (They will do the work.)
lessons.tip: In everyday speech, Brazilians often prefer 'ir + infinitive' (vou falar) over the simple future (falarei), but both are correct.

quiz.question: What is the 'eu' future form of 'falar'?
What is the irregular future stem of 'fazer'?

lessons.title: Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns
lessons.explanation: Direct object pronouns (me, te, o/a, nos, vos, os/as) replace the direct object; indirect object pronouns (me, te, lhe, nos, vos, lhes) replace the indirect object ('to/for someone'). Placement varies: before the verb (common in Brazilian Portuguese), after the verb with a hyphen (European, formal), or attached with a contraction in some verb forms.
examples: Eu o vejo todos os dias. (I see him every day.) — direct object
Ela me deu o livro. (She gave me the book.) — indirect object
Nós vamos visitá-los amanhã. (We are going to visit them tomorrow.)
Dei-lhe um presente. (I gave him/her a gift.) — European
lessons.tip: 'Lhe/lhes' are indirect object pronouns (to him/her/them); 'o/a/os/as' are direct object pronouns (him/her/it/them).

quiz.question: Which pronoun is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him/her'?
Which pronoun is a direct object pronoun meaning 'them' (masc.)?

lessons.title: Future Subjunctive — Futuro do Conjuntivo
lessons.explanation: Portuguese has a future subjunctive — rare in other Romance languages. Used after 'se' (if), 'quando' (when), 'enquanto' (while), 'assim que' (as soon as) to express future conditions. Formed from the personal infinitive.
examples: Quando chegar, telefona. (When you arrive, call.) — se+falar
Se tiveres tempo, vem. (If you have time, come.)
Enquanto estiveres aqui, aproveita. (While you are here, enjoy it.)
Assim que acabar, diz-me. (As soon as you finish, tell me.)
lessons.tip: English uses present tense after 'when/if' for future events; Portuguese uses the future subjunctive.

quiz.question: What tense does Portuguese use after 'quando' for future events?

lessons.title: Presente do Conjuntivo — Present Subjunctive
lessons.explanation: The present subjunctive expresses doubt, wish, emotion, or uncertainty after expressions like 'espero que', 'é importante que', 'duvido que'. It is formed from the 'eu' present indicative form: drop the -o and add opposite vowel endings (-AR verbs get -e endings; -ER/-IR verbs get -a endings).
examples: Espero que você venha. (I hope you come.)
É importante que estudemos. (It's important that we study.)
Duvido que ele saiba a resposta. (I doubt he knows the answer.)
Talvez ela esteja certa. (Maybe she is right.)
lessons.tip: Take the 'eu' present form, drop the -o, then flip the vowel: falar→falo→fale; comer→como→coma.

quiz.question: Which expression triggers the present subjunctive?
What is the present subjunctive 'eu/ele' form of 'falar'?

lessons.title: Voz Passiva — Passive Voice
lessons.explanation: The Portuguese passive voice is formed with ser (conjugated) plus a past participle, which agrees in gender and number with the subject. The agent, if mentioned, is introduced with 'por'.
examples: A casa é construída por um arquiteto famoso. (The house is built by a famous architect.)
O livro foi escrito por ela. (The book was written by her.)
As cartas são enviadas todos os dias. (The letters are sent every day.)
A porta foi aberta. (The door was opened.)
lessons.tip: There's also a common 'passiva pronominal' using 'se' (Vende-se casas — Houses are sold) that avoids naming an agent at all.

quiz.question: Which verb is the standard auxiliary for the Portuguese passive voice?
Which preposition introduces the agent in a passive sentence?

lessons.title: Futuro do Pretérito — Conditional Mood
lessons.explanation: The conditional (futuro do pretérito) expresses hypothetical actions ('would') or polite requests, formed by adding endings (-ia, -ias, -ia, -íamos, -íeis, -iam) directly to the infinitive. It shares irregular stems with the future tense (fazer→far-, dizer→dir-, trazer→trar-).
examples: Eu falaria com ela. (I would speak with her.)
Gostaria de um café, por favor. (I would like a coffee, please.)
Se tivesse tempo, viajaria. (If I had time, I would travel.)
Você poderia me ajudar? (Could you help me?)
lessons.tip: The conditional endings are identical to the imperfect endings of -ER/-IR verbs, but they attach to the full infinitive instead of a verb stem.

quiz.question: What is the 'eu' conditional form of 'falar'?
What is the irregular conditional stem of 'fazer'?
